node.name: Writing as Struggle: Process after AI (Session 1) | Writing as Doubt: A Talk and Workshop with Meghan O'Gieblyn
node.descriptionText:
Meghan O’Gieblyn is the author of "Will & Attention" and "God Human Animal Machine." She will be introduced by Joanna Biggs ("The Yale Review"); workshop activites after the talk will be facilitated by Steve Shoemaker (English, Yale University).

Abstract: The struggle of writing is primarily the struggle against oneself. It’s a practice that compels us to reckon with our inner doubleness, a discipline that reveals just how little we understand about what we know, what we believe, and who we are. The ability to dialogue with oneself is not only the basis of good writing; it is also the necessary foundation of a moral life. Writing, at its best, is an ongoing conversation we have with ourselves, one that shapes our thinking and our character and is never entirely resolved.

Agenda:
9:50-10:00 a.m.: Opening remarks
10:00-11:30 a.m.: Talk and workshop activities

Coffee and pastries will be provided starting at 9:30 a.m. Lunch will be available after the talk.

Note: If you wish to attend other sessions, please be sure to sign up separately as we have capacity limits. For the full schedule, see the workshop website: https://campuspress.yale.edu/struggle/schedule/

node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: Lunch and Learn with Austin Baik '11
node.descriptionText:
The Asian Network at Yale (ANY) invites you to join a conversation with Austin Baik ’11.  Austin Baik is the President of the Association of Asian American Yale Alumni. A native San Franciscan, Austin has volunteered and worked in local politics, and has spent the majority of his professional experience in Silicon Valley.

Currently, he is a Product Manager at Apple focused on the AI/ML Platforms.  Previously he drove Responsible AI and algorithmic transparency strategy at TikTok, and prior to that managed enterprise engineering programs focused on optimizing people operations through technological innovations at Meta.  Austin has also led client-facing teams across Asia-Pacific and North America for several open-source technologies software companies and possess extensive experience in information retrieval, recommender systems, and streaming analytics software.

node.name: POSTPONED Launch of Currents: Our Planet in Perspective
node.foodDetails: Catering from La Cucina de Sandra
node.descriptionText:
YSE faculty, staff, and students are invited to join the third year of a YSE dialogue series designed to strengthen our ability to engage across differences—through good food, meaningful conversation, and a sense of community. Together, we’ll build mutual respect, empathy, and courage as we navigate the complex societal challenges and opportunities that shape our shared experience.

In this opening session, we’ll use facilitation techniques to explore ways of fostering constructive dialogue within our community. Future sessions will bring together faculty, students, and staff to collaboratively build skills in deep listening, storytelling, and communicating through conflict.

No prior background or subject matter expertise is needed—just curiosity, openness, and a willingness to participate. This series has been shaped by input from students, staff, and faculty, and all members of the YSE community are warmly encouraged to join.

Facilitation provided by the Currents Committee including: Melanie Quigley, Associate Dean, Strategic Initiatives, Pete Raymond, Oastler Professor of Biogeochemistry; Co-Director, Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture, Chenee Gallaher, Director of Student Community Engagement, Analee Josselyn MEM '27, Aaliyah Chavez MEM '27, and Naurica Encarnación MEM '27.

node.descriptionText: Designing your own course but don’t know where to start? node.name: Geospatial CoP: How to Make a Map in 2 Hours
node.descriptionText:
Join us for an introduction to map making using modern digital tools. We will briefly explore the concept of what a map is and how we use digital data to represent the geospatial world. The bulk of the workshop will be spent creating a map using the geospatial tool of your choice: ArcGIS Pro, QGIS, or the R software language. We will cover aligning geospatial data (coordinate reference systems), map elements (scale bars, north arrows, legends), and changing visuals (editing symbology). It's a great opportunity to create a map for an upcoming paper or presentation, the workshop is a good entry for those wanting quick, simple results before exploring more advanced geospatial coursework.

Please fill in this form after registration: https://forms.gle/7kS62qknbCQNBA8S9

node.name: Interwoven: Sounds and Visions from the World’s Refugee Camps
node.descriptionText:
This retrospective exhibition of community art and traditional music will be on view at the Yale Institute of Sacred Music’s Miller Hall at 406 Prospect Street, New Haven from October 15 -December 3 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 12 - 4 p.m., except for Thanksgiving week when the ISM is closed.

Presented by Artolution, an international community-based public arts, education, and mental health organization that uses creative expression to build connection, resilience, and community, the exhibition is organized by Dr. Max Frieder, Artolution Co-Founder and Chief Creative Officer (read more about Dr. Frieder below).

Building on the acclaimed exhibition Interwoven: Exchange Artworks Made Between Refugee Camps Around the World, originally launched at the United Nations, this expanded presentation hosted at the ISM brings together large-scale collaborative artworks, video documentation of traditional folkloric musicians, and cultural artifacts created by displaced communities across five continents.

The exhibition creates a dialogue between visual art and music in contexts of displacement and crisis. Alongside the artworks, visitors encounter videos of musicians from the same communities, offering an opportunity to experience not only the remarkable stories behind the works, but also the sounds, movements, languages, rhythms, and creative traditions of the people who made them.

Together, these works offer a powerful portrait of communities using art, music, and cultural expression to preserve identity, share their stories, and create connections across borders.

node.name: Human Rights Workshop: A.D. Lewis , "Lawyering Against the Cisgender State"
node.descriptionText:
Lunch Provided / RSVP Required. Email the Schell Center at schell.law@yale.edu to request background readings a week prior to talk.

A.D. Sean Lewis (he/him) is a lawyer who has been organizing racial, gender, economic, and disability justice for over a decade. He is a Senior Attorney at Lambda Legal where he works on a range of transgender rights issues. Prior to joining Lambda, A.D. founded the Trans Beyond Bars Project at the Prison Law Office where he challenged discriminatory and dangerous conditions of confinement on behalf of LGBTQIA+ people in California prisons and jails. Outside of his paid work, A.D. organizes across prison walls with California Coalition for Women Prisoners and ARC Gender Justice to support incarcerated jailhouse lawyers and advocates. A.D. graduated from Stanford Law and is a member of the California State Bar.

node.name: Writing as Struggle: Process after AI (Session 2) |  Being a Thing that is Created: A Talk and Workshop with Sheila Heti
node.descriptionText:
Sheila Heti is the author of "Alphabetical Diaries," "Motherhood," and "How Should a Person Be?" She will be introduced by Noreen Khawaja (Religious Studies, Yale University). 

Abstract: A discussion around the idea that not only are AIs created consciousnesses, but so are we. This session will include the presentation of some material that Sheila Heti has been playing with in the attempt to write a book about and with “Alice,” the chatbot she communicated with in 2022. She will discuss the difficulties of using this material in making art, and why working with A.I. has made the book-writing process more, not less, difficult.

Lunch will be available beforehand, from 11:30 a.m.-12:30 p.m. Coffee will be provided after the session.

Note: If you wish to attend other sessions, please be sure to sign up separately as we have capacity limits. For the full schedule, see the workshop website: https://campuspress.yale.edu/struggle/schedule/

node.name: CLS Brown Bag Series: Panel by Jonas Elbousty (11/12/26)
node.descriptionText:
Please join us for our weekly Brown Bag on Thursday, November 12th from 1:00 p.m. – 2:00 p.m in the Dixwell Yale Community Learning Center (DYCLC). This week will be a panel organized and moderated by Jonas Elbousty.

Academic Publishing, Research Funding, and Educational Resource Development 

This panel will explore avenues for academic publishing and research funding. Panelists will share insights into identifying appropriate journals to publish, understanding research ethics and institutional Review Board (IRB). The discussion will also highlight the development and publication of educational materials, including Open Educational Resources and instructional readers. Overall, drawing on the diverse experiences of the panelists, this panel focuses on the process of writing and publishing. 

Theresa Schenker 
Jorge Méndez-Seijas 
Noelia Sánchez Walker 
Angela Lee-Smith 

Jonas Elbousty, Organized and Moderator

node.name: Teaching & Learning Discussion | Distinctly Human: Teaching Disciplinary Skills and Mitigating AI Learning Loss
node.descriptionText:
As the landscape of AI continues to change rapidly, many of us find ourselves asking how we can continue to center the human in the classroom. How do we teach core disciplinary skills, mitigate learning loss, and reflect meaningfully on AI’s relationship to these things? What do we value humans doing, whether AI can do it or not? 

Our conversation will begin with insights from Brett Smith, Senior Lecturer in Mathematics and Jill Campbell, Professor of English. They will share their own thoughts and pedagogical practices and then invite others into the conversation. Participants are encouraged to come ready to contribute their own questions, challenges, and variations on practices related to teaching core disciplinary skills. Lunch will be provided. We are committed to hosting inclusive and accessible events that allow all participants to fully engage. Please contact us at faculty.teaching@yale.edu if there are ways we can support accommodations and access needs, be aware of any dietary restrictions, or for other questions.
